problem: Zero-shot LLM/VLM VLN agents such as NavGPT, MapGPT and NavCoT caption every candidate viewpoint with a VLM and query an LLM at every step. This 'full slow-brain' loop costs many tokens and has high latency, which blocks real-time deployment.
motivation: Humans plan slowly once (parse the instruction, set subgoals), then execute quickly on perceptual intuition. They fall back to slow reasoning only when confidence drops. Zero-shot VLN has not used this slow–fast split, so an internal confidence signal that decides when to call the LLM could cut cost while keeping success rate.
key_idea: An LLM planner emits a chain of (target object, skill, imagined object graph) subgoals. A cheap detector-based fast navigator executes these subgoals. The LLM is re-invoked only when an attributed-graph-alignment confidence between the perceived and imagined object graphs falls below a threshold.
insight:
Most per-step LLM/VLM calls are redundant once a structured plan exists. Grounding it with a detector-built object graph plus a graph-matching confidence removes much of the LLM cost: L-Tok drops from 13.10k (SF-Nav, LLM every step) to 9.94k on R2R, and T-Time from 39.36 s to 26.16 s. The price is SR (41.3 → 38.2). The threshold ablation on a 300-trajectory R2R subset shows a clear accuracy–efficiency knob:
- τ=1.0: SR 39.67, 12.58k tokens, 28.08 s
- τ=0.85–0.95: SR 36.67, ~10.5k tokens, ~22 s
- τ=0.4: SR 29.67, 9.51k tokens, 19.64 s

The module ablation on the same subset (GPT-4o) splits the roles. The object–skill pairing drives success (SR 32 → 45.67 alone). The imagined chain mainly saves tokens (13.29k → 10.13k) and actually lowers SR when combined (45.67 → 37).
method: Slow LLM Planner (Π_slow): a 3-stage prompted LLM pipeline. f_goal extracts the final target object o_goal (stop condition). f_policy(I, history H, perceived graph G^p_t) outputs a reasoning trace R_t and the immediate (object, skill) subgoal. f_chain converts R_t into N future subgoals (o, sk, imagined object graph G^i).

Perceived object graph: at each step a single lightweight open-vocabulary detection (Grounding-DINO) on the current view builds a star-topology attributed graph. An agent/timestep node links to object nodes carrying label, relative 3D position and last-seen timestamp; edges carry distance and bearing. No per-viewpoint VLM captioning is done.

Fast Reactive Navigator (π_fast): a reactive policy maps the perceived graph, target object and skill (e.g., approach, go through, go up/down) to a low-level action. It greedily maximizes alignment with the subgoal's imagined graph.

Slow–Fast Bridge: estimates 2×2 edge co-occurrence probability matrices P (timestep–timestep via shared objects) and Q (timestep–object) between the perceived and imagined graph sequences (Algorithm 1). It then computes ψ_a and plugs them into an attributed-graph-alignment error bound P(A) ≤ exp(−2 log n + 2mψ_a + 2np11). Confidence is C_t = 1 − P(A).

Asynchronous triggering: if C_t ≤ τ_C, the planner appends reached subgoals to history and re-plans via f_policy + f_chain. Otherwise the fast navigator keeps executing the existing chain without any LLM call.

numbers_note:
The paper never states which split (val-unseen assumed) or how many episodes the main R2R/REVERIE tables use. Main-table rows are therefore marked 'subset' as a caution flag, not a confirmed fact. Baseline rows (NavGPT, MapGPT with GPT-4; NavCoT fine-tuned Llama) appear to be taken from the prior papers, so backbones and eval sets differ from the own GPT-4o rows. Token counts are printed with a 'k' suffix and stored as thousands (keys *_k). The confidence threshold used for the main-table SFCo-Nav rows is not given. The 300-trajectory ablation subset (Tables III/IV) is a different set from the main table. Table III threshold rows on that subset:
- SFCo-Nav-1.0: SR 39.67, OSR 49, SPL 37.08, U-Tok 12.58k, T-Time 28.08
- SFCo-Nav-0.95: SR 36.67, OSR 50.33, SPL 34.10, U-Tok 10.55k, T-Time 22.5
- SFCo-Nav-0.85: SR 36.67, OSR 50.33, SPL 34.03, U-Tok 10.42k, T-Time 22.2
- SFCo-Nav-0.6: SR 33.33, OSR 48.33, SPL 31.22, U-Tok 9.77k, T-Time 20.34
- SFCo-Nav-0.4: SR 29.67, OSR 45, SPL 27.39, U-Tok 9.51k, T-Time 19.64

The real-robot hotel-suite study is qualitative only (figure).
results: On R2R, SFCo-Nav (GPT-4o) reaches SR 38.2 / SPL 32.54 / NE 6.04. This is close to MapGPT (GPT-4) at SR 38.8 / SPL 25.8, with higher SPL. It uses 13.54k unified tokens vs 29.26k and 26.16 s total time vs 107.01 s, i.e. about 4× faster. On REVERIE it gets SR 31.33 / SPL 27.01, beating MapGPT (28.4 / 14.5) at 24.96 s vs 92.57 s, about 3.7× faster. Its own always-LLM variant SF-Nav is more accurate (R2R SR 41.3, REVERIE SR 35.87) but about 33% slower, so the confidence trigger trades some success for efficiency.
limitations: Efficiency gains cost accuracy relative to the paper's own always-LLM variant (SR drops 3.1 points on R2R and 4.5 points on REVERIE). Adding the imagined chain lowers SR from 45.67 to 37 vs the object–skill-only variant in the GPT-4o ablation.

Evaluation protocol is under-specified: split, episode count and chosen threshold are not stated, and the stop condition may use GT goal distance. Baselines use GPT-4 (NavCoT a tuned Llama) while the own method uses GPT-4o. Vision timing compares Grounding-DINO to BLIP-2, so accuracy and efficiency comparisons are not strictly apples-to-apples.

The confidence is derived from an upper bound on alignment error borrowed from attributed-graph-alignment theory, applied heuristically to tiny star graphs. Real-world validation is a single qualitative hotel-suite case study.
